title: Intonation in questions and tags
what: rising on every question, or not using a fall on question tags that ask for agreement ('It's cold, isn't it?')
summary: This intonation error often persists because it doesn't impede comprehension, yet it can subtly convey uncertainty or a lack of conviction. It costs the speaker nuance and authority in their communication, potentially undermining their message.
listenFor: Pay attention to whether your voice consistently rises at the end of all questions, especially tag questions seeking agreement.
drills: The new regulations are quite complex, aren't they?
When will the board review the proposed budget?
You've completed the analysis, haven't you?
How do we ensure compliance with these guidelines?
This strategy seems viable, doesn't it?
What challenges do you anticipate in the next phase?
We should finalize this by tomorrow, shouldn't we?
Why did they decide to restructure the department?
The presentation went well, didn't it?

probes.sentence: What is the most effective way to communicate this change?
The project deadline is next week, isn't it?
How will these adjustments impact our long-term objectives?
You've already submitted the revised proposal, haven't you?
When do you expect to receive feedback from the stakeholders?
This approach offers a clear advantage, doesn't it?

stress.text: The committee will convene next Tuesday to discuss the merger.
stress.marked: The comMITTEE will conVENE next TUESday to disCUSS the MERger.
stress.note: Main stress falls on key content words, emphasizing new or important information.

stress.text: We need to prioritize tasks to meet the impending deadline.
stress.marked: We NEED to PRIORitize TASKS to MEET the imPENDing DEADline.
stress.note: Stress highlights the crucial elements of the statement.

stress.text: The financial implications of this decision are substantial.
stress.marked: The fiNANcial imPLIcations of this deCISion are subSTANtial.
stress.note: Longer words often have internal stress patterns that contribute to overall sentence rhythm.

stress.text: Have you considered all the potential risks involved?
stress.marked: HAVE you conSIDered all the poTENtial RISKS inVOLVED?
stress.note: In questions, stress often falls on the auxiliary verb or the main verb/noun.

stress.text: It's imperative that we maintain a high level of confidentiality.
stress.marked: It's imPERative that we mainTAIN a HIGH level of conFIdenTIALity.
stress.note: Stress emphasizes words carrying significant meaning or urgency.

stress.text: The new software significantly streamlines our workflow.
stress.marked: The NEW SOFTware sigNIFicantly STREAMlines our WORKflow.
stress.note: Stress helps to distinguish between new and old information, or to highlight contrast.

stress.text: What are the key takeaways from the market research?
stress.marked: WHAT are the KEY takeAways from the MARket REsearch?
stress.note: Wh-words and important nouns/adjectives typically receive primary stress in questions.

stress.text: This initiative requires a collaborative effort from all departments.
stress.marked: This iNITiative reQUIRES a colLABorative EFfort from all dePARTments.
stress.note: Stress patterns guide the listener to the most important parts of the message.
